The ancient city Bhaktapur lies on the Eastern part of Kathmandu valley which is also known as Bhadgaon or Khwopa, Bhaktapur. It is regarded as the abode of traditional Nepali culture, custom and unique arts of wooden and potteries. The historical monument on around signifies medieval age culture and tradition of Nepal and this old city is inhabited by indigenous Newari people in large group. The main attractive monuments are Nyatapola Temple, statue of King Bhupatindra Malla, Peacock Window, Golden Gate and fifty-five windowed palace of Bhaktapur Durbar Square.
The Golden Gate is said to be the most beautiful and richly molded specimen of its kind in the entire world. The door is surmounted by a figure of the Hindu goddess Kali and Garuda (mythical griffin) and attended by two heavenly nymphs. It is embellished with monsters and other Hindu mythical creatures of marvelous intricacy. Percy Brown, an eminent English art critic and historian, described the Golden Gate as "the most lovely piece of art in the whole Kingdom; it is placed like a jewel, flashing innumerable facets in the handsome setting of its surroundings." The gate was erected by King Ranjit Malla and is the entrance to the main courtyard of the palace of fifty-five windows.

Taleju Bhawani Temple
Taleju Bhawani Temple is a magnificent architectural and spiritual landmark located in the Kathmandu Durbar Square of Nepal. Built during the Malla dynasty in 1564 by King Mahendra Malla, it is dedicated to the goddess Taleju Bhawani, the royal deity of the Malla kings. The temple is not only a place of worship but also a symbol of Nepal’s rich cultural heritage and artistic excellence.

The temple's three-tiered pagoda-style structure stands majestically on a high plinth. Its intricate wooden carvings and metalwork reflect the finest craftsmanship of the medieval period. The main deity of the temple, Taleju Bhawani, is revered as a protector of the nation, and her blessings are sought by devotees during special ceremonies. However, the temple opens to the public only once a year during the Dashain festival, adding an aura of exclusivity and sanctity to the shrine.

Surrounded by smaller shrines and stone sculptures, the temple is a visual representation of Nepalese religious art. It also holds historical significance, as it symbolizes the blending of religion, politics, and culture during the Malla era. The temple is a UNESCO World Heritage site, attracting tourists and devotees alike.

In conclusion, the Taleju Bhawani Temple is more than just a religious monument. It is a testament to Nepal's glorious history, architectural ingenuity, and spiritual depth, making it an invaluable treasure for the nation and the world.

The Taleju Bhawani Temple, located in the heart of Kathmandu Durbar Square, is an extraordinary piece of Nepalese history and culture. This beautiful temple is dedicated to the powerful goddess Taleju Bhawani, who was worshipped by the Malla kings. Its historical significance and architectural beauty make it one of the most important landmarks in the square. However, the temple is only open to the public for a brief period during the Dashain festival, particularly on the occasion of Vijaya Dashami, which adds to the temple’s mystique.

Built by King Mahendra Malla in 1563, the temple's design is a masterful representation of traditional Newari craftsmanship. The intricate wooden carvings and gilded copper roofs reflect the rich cultural heritage of the Kathmandu Valley. The three-tiered pagoda structure is said to be built in the shape of a Yantra and is supported by twelve massive steps, symbolizing the lower slopes of Mount Meru. Surrounding the main temple are sixteen smaller shrines, which enhance the spiritual significance of the site.

Even though visitors can't enter the temple except during Dashain, the exterior is breathtaking. The temple's ornate wood carvings, symbolic toranas above the doorways, and the detailed artistry on the false and real doors showcase the incredible skills of the artisans from the Malla period. The roofs, covered in gilt copper sheets, give the structure an aura of grandeur and reverence.

The temple holds immense religious importance for the Hindu community in Nepal, especially during Durga Puja. During this festival, thousands of devotees come to pay homage to Taleju Bhawani. If you're lucky enough to visit during this time, it's a truly sacred experience. The rest of the year, visitors can still admire the temple’s grandeur from the outside, which is well worth the visit, even if access to the interior is restricted.

Overall, the Taleju Bhawani Temple is a must-visit for those interested in Nepalese culture and history. The combination of its religious significance, stunning architecture, and connection to the Malla dynasty make it a true gem of Kathmandu Durbar Square.

The Taleju Temple is one of Hanuman Dhoka Darbar Square's oldest structures. A "great temple" was built in 1563, under Mahendra Malla's rule, according to ancient diaries (tyasaphus) (r. 1560-74). Four notable structures, including the Jagannath, Kotilingeswar Mahadev, and Mahendreswara temples, are known to have been constructed at Darbar Square under the reign of Mahendra Malla. The Malla period building spree was financed by the kingdom's efforts to issue Tibetan currency for export and increase trade with other Himalayan kingdoms. The temple's current design resembles a cosmic mandala. The main structure has three levels of roofing and is supported by a base with twelve steps that resembles Mount Meru's lower slopes. There are sixteen satellite shrines built as two-story Newar towers all around the sanctuary. Notably, the main structure's roofs are covered in gilt copper sheets and supported by wooden struts with carvings of many gods. The temple is accessed by four portals—one on each side—each of which has a true door and two false doors. With carved wooden colonnettes, toranas over the main doorways, and pointed blocks (bhailahkva) flanking the lower door jambs, each is elaborately articulated.

This Bihar was built in the year 1707 during the reign of King Bhupatindra Malla. Bihar means a holy land of Buddhism. Located in Bhaktapur Golmadhi, this Buddha in Bihar is one of the five Dipankara Buddhas in Bhaktapur city. Dipankar is a Sanskrit word which means to come with a lamp.  Dipankar Buddha came to this earth one hundred thousand years ago to light the lamp of knowledge. Dipankar Buddha is called Dipankha Buddha in Nepal language. The five Bihars of Dipankar in Bhaktapur are different types of Bihars in Nepal Mandal. A two-storied courtyard is built all around, while a large square is built in the middle of the courtyard. There is a stupa of Buddha in that square. A supernatural idol of Lord Dipankar is placed in one of the rooms of Sat, while a five-sided window is placed above the main entrance. Built in a very peaceful environment, this place has been built in an environment that makes you want to go again once you visit it. The three chaityas in the middle add to the beauty of this place. Among those three Chaityas are Tathagata Akshovya, Bajradhatu Chaitya, and Sikgrara Chaitya. Apart from this, idols of Shri Ganesha and Mahakal have also been installed. On the day of Bhadra Krishna Trayodashi, Jatra is held here during Panchdan Maha Parva and Jatra is also held on the day of Magh Sakranti. And also there is a special fair held in Gunla for a month. Previously Ranjitkars used to perform daily bhajan, but on Sakimana Purnima day Ranjitkars also perform Halimali (God of bread).

The Uma Maheshwor Temple in Kirtipur, Nepal, is a sacred site that holds great cultural and religious significance. Dedicated to the Hindu deities Shiva and Parvati (known as Maheshwor and Uma in their divine forms), this ancient temple is a popular pilgrimage destination for devotees and tourists alike.

The temple's architecture reflects traditional Newari craftsmanship and design, with intricate woodcarvings, pagoda-style roofs, and ornate metalwork decorating its exterior. As visitors approach the temple, they are greeted by a sense of peace and tranquility, enhanced by the serene surroundings and views of the Kathmandu Valley.

Inside the temple complex, devotees offer prayers, light oil lamps, and perform rituals to seek blessings from Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati. The temple is also known for its annual festivals and religious ceremonies, which attract large crowds of worshippers and spectators.

Apart from its religious significance, the Uma Maheshwor Temple is also a symbol of Nepal's rich cultural heritage and architectural prowess. The site's historical importance is underscored by its preservation efforts and ongoing maintenance, ensuring that future generations can continue to appreciate and cherish this sacred place.

Ultimately, the Uma Maheshwor Temple in Kirtipur stands as a testament to the enduring spiritual beliefs and architectural legacy of the Nepalese people, offering a glimpse into the country's vibrant past and continuing traditions

Nil Barahi Temple, known as निल बराही मन्दिर in Nepali, is a revered Hindu temple located on the banks of the Phewa Lake in Pokhara, Nepal. It is dedicated to Goddess Barahi, who is worshipped as a protector and provider of strength to devotees.

The temple is situated on a small island within Phewa Lake, accessible by boats operated from the lakeside. This serene and picturesque setting adds to the spiritual ambiance of the temple, making it a popular pilgrimage site and tourist attraction in Pokhara.

Goddess Barahi is depicted with the head of a boar and the body of a woman, symbolizing her protective and nurturing qualities. She is considered a manifestation of Goddess Durga, revered for her power and ability to overcome obstacles and challenges.

Devotees visit Nil Barahi Temple to seek blessings from Goddess Barahi, particularly for protection from harm, success in endeavors, and overall well-being. Special prayers and rituals are performed by priests and devotees, especially during festivals and auspicious occasions.

The temple complex includes the main shrine of Goddess Barahi, surrounded by smaller shrines dedicated to other Hindu deities. It also features open spaces where devotees can perform rituals, light oil lamps, and offer prayers amidst the natural beauty of Phewa Lake and the surrounding hills.

In addition to its religious significance, Nil Barahi Temple offers stunning views of Phewa Lake and the Annapurna mountain range, making it a tranquil and scenic destination for visitors exploring Pokhara. Boat rides to the temple provide an opportunity for spiritual reflection and appreciation of Nepal's natural beauty.

Overall, Nil Barahi Temple holds cultural, religious, and natural significance in Pokhara, Nepal, attracting pilgrims, tourists, and nature enthusiasts alike. It stands as a symbol of faith, devotion, and reverence for Goddess Barahi and continues to be a cherished spiritual sanctuary in the region.

text: One of the four kumaris revered in the Kathmandu Valley is Balkumari of Madhyapur Thimi. She is revered by the locals as their protector deity. There, the natives hold rites for their daily lives including weddings and Barthabandha. A rectangular courtyard with brick pavers surrounds the Balkumari temple. Moreover, it contains both small and important deities, such as the Digu Bhairava shrine. The history of the temple is extensive and almost begins in the 17th century. Of sure, as it was the period the temple was built. According to folklore, a businessman from Madhyapur frequently traveled with his gang to Lubu for commercial purposes. But someway, both he and the princess of the Lubu, fell in love. The princess soon became pregnant as well. She requested that the merchant take her to the thimi as a result. The merchant gladly agreed to her proposition, but he also included a caveat. She had to bring the balkumari with her if she wanted to travel to Thimi with him. The princess did so with joy as well, bringing the deity to the thimi. The god was then permanently relocated to Thimi. Moreover, a womb-like structure is located directly above the deity's idol. This in some ways supports the myth about the pregnant women moving the deity.

Cultural preservation is crucial in this modern day world.

This Chyasin Mandap was completely destroyed in the earthquake of 1934 A.D. The present structure was reconstructed in 1989 A.D., with
the assistance of the German Government. It was reconstructed to commemorate the visit of Chancellor Helmut Kohl to Bhaktapur: Poke your head inside and note the earthquake resistant steel-beams on the
lower level. There has been much controversy over their construction. Local craftsmen complained that these beams destroyed the ritual efficacy of the Mandap because the use of metal in temple construction is ritually prohibited, and that they should at least be covered in wood.

And it is rumored that the American First Lady Hillary Clinton, when she was given a tour of the site also questioned their aesthetic value.

Taleju bell or Big bell is installed north of chyasi deval (Octagonal Krishna Mandir). This bell is also called Taleju bell because it is installed in the vicinity of Taleju temple. Taleju was considered to be the family goddess or Kuldevi of the then Mall royal family. The big bell made from cast iron is hanging between two stout pillars & was placed by King Vishnu Malla in 1736 after the earlier bell donated in 1703 was moved to the Rato Machhindranath Temple. During that time, this bell used to be rung in order to signal incoming invaders, and to make royal and other important announcements. Another idea for its construction was that Petitioners (citizens) could ring the bell to alert the king to their grievances.

Changu Narayan, perched atop a high hill in the Changunarayan Municipality of Bhaktapur District, Nepal, is an ancient Hindu temple dedicated to Lord Vishnu. The temple survived destruction in 1702 and the 2015 earthquake, standing as Nepal’s oldest functional Hindu temple within the Kathmandu Valley. Visitors ascend the hill, passing lush greenery and stone sculptures, creating an otherworldly experience. Changu Narayan’s enduring legacy and UNESCO World Heritage Site status make it a captivating destination for history enthusiasts and seekers of divine grace . 🕉️

Changunarayan Temple, located near Kathmandu in Nepal, is a cultural jewel steeped in history and artistry. This ancient Hindu temple, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, showcases exquisite stone carvings, intricate woodwork, and impressive architecture dating back to the 4th century. Devotees and tourists are captivated by the temple's serene atmosphere and the spiritual aura that permeates its surroundings. The temple premises are adorned with sculptures depicting various deities, mythological beings, and scenes from Hindu epics, providing a glimpse into Nepal's rich cultural heritage. The temple's strategic hilltop location offers stunning views of the Kathmandu Valley, enhancing the overall experience. Changunarayan Temple stands as a testament to Nepal's artistic heritage and religious significance, making it a must-visit destination for history enthusiasts and spiritual seekers alike.

Nyatapola Temple 🙏🏼🫰🏼🇳🇵

The Nyatapola Temple is situated in Nepal’s Bhaktapur. This iconic building from the turn of the 18th century is the tallest temple in Nepal, rising to a height of more than 30 meters. The lovely brick and wood structure, resembling a pagoda, was dubbed Nyatapola, derived from the Newari terms for “roof” (pola) and “five-stepped” (nyata). It was lavishly carved.

Source: Atlas Obscura

Visiting the Nyatapola Temple in Bhaktapur's Durbar Square nearly two decades ago was an unforgettable experience. This towering five-storied pagoda, the tallest in Nepal, captivated me with its intricate carvings and sheer grandeur. Set within the enchanting Durbar Square, with its array of temples and palaces, the Nyatapola  stands out as a true architectural masterpiece. Even after all these years, I vividly remember the sense of awe and admiration I felt. It's a must-see destination for any visitor to Nepal.

The 55 Window Palace, also known as Pachpanna Jhyale Durbar in Nepali, is a historic palace located in Bhaktapur Durbar Square in Bhaktapur, Nepal. It was built during the reign of King Bhupatindra Malla in the 15th century and is considered one of the finest examples of traditional Newari architecture in Nepal.

The palace is named after its 55 intricately carved wooden windows, which are adorned with lattice work, statues of deities, and other decorative elements. The palace was originally used as a royal residence and a center for administration, and it was also the site of important ceremonies and events.

The 55 Window Palace is a three-story building with a central courtyard and a number of smaller rooms and chambers. The palace is built entirely from brick and timber, and its sloping roofs and ornate carvings are typical of Newari architecture. The palace is now a museum, where visitors can learn about the history of Bhaktapur and the Malla dynasty.

In addition to the 55 Window Palace, Bhaktapur Durbar Square is home to a number of other important structures, including the Golden Gate, the Taleju Temple, and the Natapole Temple, among others. The area is also known for its vibrant street life, with vendors selling traditional handicrafts, food, and other goods in the bustling squares and alleyways. Overall, Bhaktapur Durbar Square is a must-visit destination for anyone interested in Nepal's rich cultural heritage and history.

The 55 Window Palace (also known as Pachpanchhya Jhale) is a palace located in Bhaktapur Durbar Square, Nepal. It is a five-story palace with 55 intricately carved windows, hence the name. The palace was built in the 17th century by King Bhupatindra Malla and is considered one of the finest examples of Newari architecture.
The windows of the palace are made of sandalwood and are decorated with intricate carvings of flowers, animals, and other motifs. The palace also has a number of other features, including a courtyard, a water tank, and a library.
The 55 Window Palace was damaged in the 1934 earthquake, but it has since been restored. It is now a popular tourist destination and is one of the most photographed buildings in Bhaktapur.

KakreBihar in Surkhet District, Nepal, is a hidden gem that offers a unique blend of history, spirituality, and natural beauty. This ancient Hindu-Buddhist temple, built in the 12th century, stands majestically on a small hill in Latikoili , providing a serene and picturesque setting.

The temple’s architecture is a marvel, constructed from solid stone with intricate bronze idols of Hindu gods and goddesses, as well as Buddha. The restoration efforts completed in 2021 have beautifully preserved its historical essence while making it more accessible to visitors1. The site spans over 180 hectares, offering ample space for exploration and reflection.

Visiting KakreBihar is not just about the temple itself but also about the journey. The surrounding landscape is lush and green, with panoramic views of the Surkhet Valley. The moderate climate makes it a pleasant destination year-round. Whether you’re a history enthusiast, a spiritual seeker, or simply someone who appreciates natural beauty, KakreBihar has something to offer.

The peaceful ambiance of the temple grounds is perfect for meditation and relaxation. The local community is welcoming, and you can often find knowledgeable guides who can share fascinating stories about the temple’s history and significance. There are also several spots nearby for picnics and leisurely walks, making it a great place for families and solo travelers alike.

In summary, KakreBihar is a must-visit destination in Surkhet District. Its rich history, stunning architecture, and tranquil environment make it a perfect escape from the hustle and bustle of daily life. Highly recommended for anyone traveling through Karnali Province!

Since its discovery about 50 years ago, the Kakrebihar site has attracted the interest of archaeologists and Buddhist scholars. They agree that it dates back to the 13th-14th century, but question whether it is truly a Buddhist site or a Hindu temple that adopted Buddhist characteristics.

Was it one of the many places on the prehistoric route that passed through the Surkhet-Dang region through the vital Gangetic plains to the south? Who built it — the followers of Vajrayana Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley or the Tibetan Buddhism in the mountains? And was it also built as a temple, or could it have been a palace, monastery or something else?

Navadurga means nine forms of Durga(incarnation of goddess parvati).The names are likely to be different as you travel from place to place .In Bhakapur,the names are respectively as:Brahmayini, Maheswori, Kumari, Bhadrakali, Barahi, Indrayani, Mahakali, Mahalaxmi, Tripurasundari. The first eight goddesses are also called Astramatrikas. The temples of the Astramatrikas surrounds Bhaktapur. Tripurasundari is located nearly at the center of the core city.This tells the idea of planning in the far past.

The masks of the goddesses along with masks of Ganesh,Sima,Duma, Balkumari,Mahadev and Suti Bhairav are carved at Yachhen Tole. During the Dashain festival, the masks are taken to the Brahmayini temple and exhibited there.It is supposed to be the time when the goddesses are born. After Dashain, the goddesses are taken round the core city of Bhaktapur during night time.

The jatra then begins after Dashain from Jayabageshwori (termed as the first settlement of the Newar community). In the jatra of Navadurga, the goddesses are taken to various toles of the Kathmandu Valley and they perform their traditional dances and people are also entertained by “Nyaleke”(a game type chasing of the local boys by the goddesses Sima, Duma and Bhairav & if the boys are caught their ears are pulled and the boys pays money to the goddess). The goddesses are taken to almost many settlements of the Kathmandu Valley and also to the nearby small traditional towns like Sankhu, Nala, Bungamati, Panauti, Dhulikhel etc. The last place visited is Echhi tole (In Bhaktapur).

There is the provision of Diwali Puja at Siti Nakha (one of the festival in Newars)  in the community of the Banmala Family (Goddesses are made from this caste) where sheeps and hens are offered.

The death of the goddesses are considered on Bhagasti (On Saptami of Dilla). On this day, the masks are again taken to Brahmayani and burnt there.

Navadurga (Nine forms of Parvati, IAST: durgā), are nine manifestations of Goddess Parvati in Hinduism, especially worshiped during Navaratri and Durga Puja.[1] The nine forms of Durga are often considered collectively as a single deity, mainly among the followers of Shaktism sect of Hinduism, while the nine forms are worshipped on Nine days.[2]
According to the Hindu mythology, the nine forms are considered as the nine stages of Parvati during the nine-day long duration of the war with demon-king Mahishasura, where the tenth day is celebrated as the Vijayadashami (lit. 'Victory day') among the Hindus and is considered as one of the most important festivals along with the Navaratri.[3]
During the festival of Navratri, nine unmarried virgin girls up to the age of nine years are worshiped and fed as they are considered to be the incarnations of these nine goddesses.[4] Then, there is Nabapatrika ritual during Durga Puja involves tying the branches of eight plants with their leaves with a banana plant ("Naba" meaning nine, and "Patrika" meaning leaves).[5] The tenth day is considered as Vijayadashami, or the tenth day of victory which is on the same date as Dussehra.

Baglung Kalika Temple, a revered Hindu pilgrimage site, is located in Baglung district in the Gandaki Province of Nepal. It stands atop a scenic hill on the northern banks of the Kali Gandaki River, near the town of Baglung, around 280 kilometers west of Kathmandu. Surrounded by lush forests and overlooking stunning mountain vistas, the temple offers both spiritual and natural beauty.

Historical Significance:
Baglung Kalika is dedicated to Goddess Kali, one of the fiercest forms of Shakti in Hinduism, symbolizing power and protection. According to local legends, the temple was established centuries ago during the Malla dynasty, making it an ancient and culturally significant site. Many believe the temple was built as a protective shrine for the Baglung area, and devotees come to seek blessings for courage, success, and protection.

The annual Bada Dashain festival sees thousands of visitors and is marked by rituals, animal sacrifices, and vibrant celebrations. The temple’s history and connection with the Malla kings and various dynasties add a rich historical depth to the place, making it not just a religious site but also an important part of Nepal’s heritage.

Experience & Facilities:
Visitors often remark on the spiritual energy felt at Baglung Kalika Temple. The panoramic views of the Dhaulagiri and Annapurna ranges add a majestic backdrop to the sacred environment. The temple offers basic amenities for visitors, including water, seating areas, and small shops selling offerings. The steps leading up to the temple are well-maintained, but some may find the climb challenging.

Conclusion:
Baglung Kalika Temple is a must-visit for those interested in Nepal’s spiritual and historical landscape. The combination of its powerful atmosphere, historical roots, and natural surroundings make it a profoundly moving experience. This temple is not only a place of worship but also a window into the cultural and spiritual heart of Nepal.

One of the most intriguing features of Buda Subba Temple is its connection to local legends. Budha Subba Temple: A Cultural and Spiritual Landmark in Eastern Nepal

Located in the picturesque town of Bijayapur, Dharan, Nepal, the Budha Subba Temple is a revered and culturally significant site that attracts devotees from various backgrounds. This temple, nestled in the eastern region of Nepal, is steeped in history, mythology, and unique traditions that set it apart from other religious sites.

Location and Accessibility

The temple is situated on top of Bijayapur Hill, overlooking the Seuti River, and is approximately 220 km away from Kathmandu. Its geographic coordinates are 26.820°N 87.30°E, making it easily accessible for both local and international visitors.

Historical Significance

The Budha Subba Temple is primarily known as the tomb of King Buddhi Karnaraya Khebang, the last Limbu King of Morang. King Buddhi Karnaraya Khebang was assassinated by the assassins of King Prithvi Narayan Shah of the Kingdom of Nepal during negotiations in Bijayapur-Dharan. Despite the tragic circumstances of his death, the locals have transformed this site into a place of reverence, worshiping the king's spirit as a friendly and helpful presence believed to bring good luck.

Unique Features and Worship Practices

One of the striking features of the Budha Subba Temple is the absence of an idol, a departure from the conventional setup of many religious sites. Instead, devotees worship two earthen bases within the ancient temple, revered as Budha Subba and Budhi Subban. This unconventional aspect adds an air of mystery and uniqueness to the temple.The temple complex is also notable for its tip-less bamboo plants, a phenomenon attributed to the legend of Budha Subba. According to myth, Budha Subba, a hunter, accidentally broke the tips of the bamboo trees while hunting crows, and they never grew back.

Rituals and Offerings

Devotees flock to the temple, especially on Saturdays, to partake in rituals that involve the sacrificial offerings of animals such as pigs and chickens. These offerings are seen as gestures of devotion and expressions of gratitude to the deity, believed to have the power to fulfill wishes and bring good fortune.

Cultural and Mythological Significance

The temple is surrounded by numerous myths and legends. One legend connects the temple to Eklavya, a character from the Mahabharata, who is said to have meditated at this site. Another myth involves Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati, who allegedly arrived at Vijaypur in disguise and performed penance, leading to the bamboo sprouting without tips.The temple also holds significance for young couples, who believe that tying colorful strings around the bamboo trees and engraving their names will bring them happiness and long life together.

Atmosphere and Facilities

The temple complex offers a peaceful and meditative environment, ideal for those seeking spiritual solace. The surroundings are tranquil, and the absence of an idol creates a unique and inclusive atmosphere that attracts devotees from various religious backgrounds. The temple also features a small car parking facility and souvenir shops within the complex.

Conclusion

The Budha Subba Temple is more than just a religious site; it is a repository of history, mythology, and cultural traditions. Its unique features, diverse legends, and inclusive atmosphere make it a fascinating destination for those seeking spiritual solace and a deeper connection to the rich cultural heritage of eastern Nepal. Whether you are a local or an international visitor, the Budha Subba Temple is a must-visit site that offers a profound and enriching experience.

Taleju Bhawani Temple
Taleju Bhawani Temple is a magnificent architectural and spiritual landmark located in the Kathmandu Durbar Square of Nepal. Built during the Malla dynasty in 1564 by King Mahendra Malla, it is dedicated to the goddess Taleju Bhawani, the royal deity of the Malla kings. The temple is not only a place of worship but also a symbol of Nepal’s rich cultural heritage and artistic excellence.

The temple's three-tiered pagoda-style structure stands majestically on a high plinth. Its intricate wooden carvings and metalwork reflect the finest craftsmanship of the medieval period. The main deity of the temple, Taleju Bhawani, is revered as a protector of the nation, and her blessings are sought by devotees during special ceremonies. However, the temple opens to the public only once a year during the Dashain festival, adding an aura of exclusivity and sanctity to the shrine.

Surrounded by smaller shrines and stone sculptures, the temple is a visual representation of Nepalese religious art. It also holds historical significance, as it symbolizes the blending of religion, politics, and culture during the Malla era. The temple is a UNESCO World Heritage site, attracting tourists and devotees alike.

In conclusion, the Taleju Bhawani Temple is more than just a religious monument. It is a testament to Nepal's glorious history, architectural ingenuity, and spiritual depth, making it an invaluable treasure for the nation and the world.

The Taleju Bhawani Temple, located in the heart of Kathmandu Durbar Square, is an extraordinary piece of Nepalese history and culture. This beautiful temple is dedicated to the powerful goddess Taleju Bhawani, who was worshipped by the Malla kings. Its historical significance and architectural beauty make it one of the most important landmarks in the square. However, the temple is only open to the public for a brief period during the Dashain festival, particularly on the occasion of Vijaya Dashami, which adds to the temple’s mystique.

Built by King Mahendra Malla in 1563, the temple's design is a masterful representation of traditional Newari craftsmanship. The intricate wooden carvings and gilded copper roofs reflect the rich cultural heritage of the Kathmandu Valley. The three-tiered pagoda structure is said to be built in the shape of a Yantra and is supported by twelve massive steps, symbolizing the lower slopes of Mount Meru. Surrounding the main temple are sixteen smaller shrines, which enhance the spiritual significance of the site.

Even though visitors can't enter the temple except during Dashain, the exterior is breathtaking. The temple's ornate wood carvings, symbolic toranas above the doorways, and the detailed artistry on the false and real doors showcase the incredible skills of the artisans from the Malla period. The roofs, covered in gilt copper sheets, give the structure an aura of grandeur and reverence.

The temple holds immense religious importance for the Hindu community in Nepal, especially during Durga Puja. During this festival, thousands of devotees come to pay homage to Taleju Bhawani. If you're lucky enough to visit during this time, it's a truly sacred experience. The rest of the year, visitors can still admire the temple’s grandeur from the outside, which is well worth the visit, even if access to the interior is restricted.

Overall, the Taleju Bhawani Temple is a must-visit for those interested in Nepalese culture and history. The combination of its religious significance, stunning architecture, and connection to the Malla dynasty make it a true gem of Kathmandu Durbar Square.

The Taleju Temple is one of Hanuman Dhoka Darbar Square's oldest structures. A "great temple" was built in 1563, under Mahendra Malla's rule, according to ancient diaries (tyasaphus) (r. 1560-74). Four notable structures, including the Jagannath, Kotilingeswar Mahadev, and Mahendreswara temples, are known to have been constructed at Darbar Square under the reign of Mahendra Malla. The Malla period building spree was financed by the kingdom's efforts to issue Tibetan currency for export and increase trade with other Himalayan kingdoms. The temple's current design resembles a cosmic mandala. The main structure has three levels of roofing and is supported by a base with twelve steps that resembles Mount Meru's lower slopes. There are sixteen satellite shrines built as two-story Newar towers all around the sanctuary. Notably, the main structure's roofs are covered in gilt copper sheets and supported by wooden struts with carvings of many gods. The temple is accessed by four portals—one on each side—each of which has a true door and two false doors. With carved wooden colonnettes, toranas over the main doorways, and pointed blocks (bhailahkva) flanking the lower door jambs, each is elaborately articulated.

The Gosainkunda Trek (6-7 days from Kathmandu) is a breathtaking journey that I would highly recommend to any trekking enthusiast! Gosaikunda is a holy lake that is worshipped by the Hindus and Buddhists of Nepal and Surya Peak is situated in the north of the lake. After you reach at the peak you will be amazed by the beauty of Sarswoti Lake, Bhairab Lake, and the legendary Gosainkunda Lake.
My experience was nothing short of magical, and here’s why:
Stunning Scenery: The trek offers some of the most beautiful landscapes I've ever seen. From lush green hills to rugged mountain paths, every step was filled with awe-inspiring views. The sight of the majestic Langtang range against the backdrop of clear blue skies was a highlight that I will cherish forever.
Challenging Yet Rewarding: The trek is definitely challenging, with steep ascents and descents, especially as you approach Gosainkunda Lake. However, the effort is well worth it! Reaching the lake at an altitude of 4,380 meters felt like an incredible achievement, and the serene beauty of the lake surrounded by snow-capped peaks took my breath away.
Cultural Experience: Along the way, I had the opportunity to interact  with Sherpas and Tamangs who have different culture and you can get a chance to learn in depth about them. Their warmth and hospitality added depth to the experience. I enjoyed traditional meals at the tea houses and learned about their customs and traditions, which made the trek even more enriching.
Well-Marked Trail: The trail is well-marked, making navigation easier, even for those who may not be experienced trekkers. There are plenty of spots to stop and take breaks, and the views just get better the higher you go.
Wildlife and Nature: I was fortunate enough to see a variety of wildlife, including Himalayan monkeys and various bird species. The flora is equally impressive, with vibrant rhododendron forests that burst into color during the spring.
Accommodations: The tea houses along the route were comfortable, with friendly hosts who made me feel right at home. The food was delicious and varied, catering to both local and international tastes.
Final Thoughts: If you’re looking for a trek that combines natural beauty, cultural immersion, and a sense of adventure, the Gosainkunda Trek is the perfect choice. It’s a journey that challenges you physically while rewarding you with unforgettable memories and stunning vistas.  All you need is to be fit and healthy and the willingness and capability of walking for around 7 to 9 hours every day.

Guheshwari Temple: A Sacred Abode of Divine Power

Located just 1km east of the revered Pashupatinath Temple, on the southern bank of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Nepal, Guheshwari Temple stands as a testament to the profound spiritual heritage of the region.

At the heart of this holy site lies the deity Mahadevi Guhyekali, symbolizing the primordial Aadhi Shakti, or Divine Power. The temple's energy dynamics, intricately linked with its proximity to the Pashupatinath Temple, add to its spiritual significance, drawing devout tantric worshipers seeking divine blessings.

Originally built in the pagoda style, the temple was meticulously renovated in the 17th century by King Pratap Malla, preserving its architectural splendor for generations to come.

Guheshwari Temple comes alive during its main festivals, such as Chaitra Dashain, Bada Dashain, and Navratri, when devotees flock to pay homage to the divine feminine energy embodied within its sacred walls.

Legend intertwines with mythology at Guheshwari Temple, as it is believed to mark the spot where Sati Devi, in her fury at the disrespect shown to her husband Shiva by her father Daksha, immolated herself. Unable to bear her loss, Shiva carried her body, and as her divine form disintegrated, her body parts fell to earth, creating the 51 Shakti Peeths. Guheshwari Temple stands as a testament to this myth, marking the place where Sati Devi's hips fell, infusing the site with the divine power of the universe.

For centuries, Guheshwari Temple has been a focal point of spiritual reverence, drawing pilgrims and seekers from far and wide to bask in its divine aura and connect with the primal energy that permeates its sacred precincts.

The babies have some training to keep them and their handlers safe, which is understandable for the success of the re-wilding program. It is very clear that there is zero exploitation here.

Taleju Bhawani Temple is a magnificent architectural and spiritual landmark located in the Kathmandu Durbar Square of Nepal. Built during the Malla dynasty in 1564 by King Mahendra Malla, it is dedicated to the goddess Taleju Bhawani, the royal deity of the Malla kings. The temple is not only a place of worship but also a symbol of Nepal’s rich cultural heritage and artistic excellence.

The temple's three-tiered pagoda-style structure stands majestically on a high plinth. Its intricate wooden carvings and metalwork reflect the finest craftsmanship of the medieval period. The main deity of the temple, Taleju Bhawani, is revered as a protector of the nation, and her blessings are sought by devotees during special ceremonies. However, the temple opens to the public only once a year during the Dashain festival, adding an aura of exclusivity and sanctity to the shrine.

Surrounded by smaller shrines and stone sculptures, the temple is a visual representation of Nepalese religious art. It also holds historical significance, as it symbolizes the blending of religion, politics, and culture during the Malla era. The temple is a UNESCO World Heritage site, attracting tourists and devotees alike.

In conclusion, the Taleju Bhawani Temple is more than just a religious monument. It is a testament to Nepal's glorious history, architectural ingenuity, and spiritual depth, making it an invaluable treasure for the nation and the world.

The Taleju Bhawani Temple, located in the heart of Kathmandu Durbar Square, is an extraordinary piece of Nepalese history and culture. Its historical significance and architectural beauty make it one of the most important landmarks in the square. However, the temple is only open to the public for a brief period during the Dashain festival, particularly on the occasion of Vijaya Dashami, which adds to the temple’s mystique.

Built by King Mahendra Malla in 1563, the temple's design is a masterful representation of traditional Newari craftsmanship. The intricate wooden carvings and gilded copper roofs reflect the rich cultural heritage of the Kathmandu Valley. The three-tiered pagoda structure is said to be built in the shape of a Yantra and is supported by twelve massive steps, symbolizing the lower slopes of Mount Meru. Surrounding the main temple are sixteen smaller shrines, which enhance the spiritual significance of the site.

Even though visitors can't enter the temple except during Dashain, the exterior is breathtaking. The temple's ornate wood carvings, symbolic toranas above the doorways, and the detailed artistry on the false and real doors showcase the incredible skills of the artisans from the Malla period. The roofs, covered in gilt copper sheets, give the structure an aura of grandeur and reverence.

The temple holds immense religious importance for the Hindu community in Nepal, especially during Durga Puja. During this festival, thousands of devotees come to pay homage to Taleju Bhawani. If you're lucky enough to visit during this time, it's a truly sacred experience. The rest of the year, visitors can still admire the temple’s grandeur from the outside, which is well worth the visit, even if access to the interior is restricted.

Overall, the Taleju Bhawani Temple is a must-visit for those interested in Nepalese culture and history. The combination of its religious significance, stunning architecture, and connection to the Malla dynasty make it a true gem of Kathmandu Durbar Square.

The Taleju Temple is one of Hanuman Dhoka Darbar Square's oldest structures. A "great temple" was built in 1563, under Mahendra Malla's rule, according to ancient diaries (tyasaphus) (r. 1560-74). Four notable structures, including the Jagannath, Kotilingeswar Mahadev, and Mahendreswara temples, are known to have been constructed at Darbar Square under the reign of Mahendra Malla. The Malla period building spree was financed by the kingdom's efforts to issue Tibetan currency for export and increase trade with other Himalayan kingdoms. The temple's current design resembles a cosmic mandala. The main structure has three levels of roofing and is supported by a base with twelve steps that resembles Mount Meru's lower slopes. There are sixteen satellite shrines built as two-story Newar towers all around the sanctuary. Notably, the main structure's roofs are covered in gilt copper sheets and supported by wooden struts with carvings of many gods. The temple is accessed by four portals—one on each side—each of which has a true door and two false doors. Pachali Bhairab, situated in Teku, Kathmandu, is a revered deity in the Kathmandu Valley's Newar community. Regarded as a fierce manifestation of Lord Shiva, Bhairab embodies protection and destruction. The shrine holds immense cultural and religious significance, attracting devotees seeking blessings, protection from evil, and spiritual strength.

The temple complex is modest yet sacred, featuring an iconic idol of Bhairab adorned with metal masks, elaborate ornaments, and offerings from worshippers. The deity is associated with tantric rituals and traditional ceremonies, emphasizing its connection to local beliefs and practices. Pachali Bhairab is particularly significant during the Pachali Bhairab Jatra, an annual festival that involves elaborate processions, rituals, and celebrations. The festival showcases the deity's journey through different parts of the city, accompanied by music, dances, and the participation of the Newar community.

Pachali Bhairab's role extends beyond religious importance. It serves as a cultural hub, preserving the heritage and traditions of the Newars. The temple’s connection with various jatras and rituals demonstrates the seamless integration of spirituality and community in Newar culture. Local legends and myths surrounding Pachali Bhairab add layers of mystique, making it a subject of fascination for cultural enthusiasts and scholars.

Nestled in the historic area of Teku, near the confluence of the Bagmati and Bishnumati rivers, the location itself carries spiritual significance. Pilgrims believe that visiting the temple brings prosperity, peace, and spiritual fulfillment.

In essence, Pachali Bhairab stands as a testament to the rich cultural, religious, and historical fabric of the Kathmandu Valley. It continues to be a site of devotion and celebration, where spirituality and tradition converge harmoniously.

Tonglu is a quaint hamlet nestled between Manebhanjan and Sandakphu, and it serves as the perfect retreat to detox and explore the mountains. This place truly comes alive when the rhododendrons and magnolias are in bloom, turning Tonglu into a riot of colors. The forest is home to more than 600 varieties of orchids, filling the air with a heady, delightful fragrance.

The tranquility of the surrounding areas makes Tonglu an ideal getaway for meditation and relaxation. The night sky here, dotted with thousands of stars, creates a mesmerizing spectacle that makes up for the pitch-dark layout. Trekking back to Dhotre in the afternoon offers another chance to stroll through the enchanting sub-Alpine forest.

My visit to Tonglu was nothing short of heavenly. As my first trek, it has become one of the most memorable moments of my life. The view of Mount Kanchendzunga is crystal clear from this vantage point, offering a perfect angle to see the "Sleeping Buddha" formation from everywhere you go.

Tonglu is a small village situated atop a mountain, primarily used by trekkers en route to Sandakphu as an overnight stop. We started our trek from Dhotrey, which took approximately 4.5 hours to reach Tonglu. The homestays are clean, and the hosts are incredibly welcoming and helpful. We visited in January, and to our delight, we were greeted with a clear view of Kanchendzunga the next morning. Witnessing the sunrise here, with Kanchendzunga changing colors with the rising sun, was the most beautiful sunrise I've ever seen.

After a hearty breakfast, we took a short trek to a nearby monastery situated in the lower part of Tonglu and spent some peaceful time there. The weather was quite chilly, with temperatures near 5-6 degrees Celsius in the morning and dropping to below zero at night. The strong winds added to the cold, but the sight of the gigantic Sleeping Buddha lying in front of us made us forget the cold entirely.

The Mahabuddha Temple in Lalitpur, Nepal, stands as a serene testament to the country's rich cultural and religious heritage. This architectural marvel, dating back to the 17th century, showcases exquisite craftsmanship and intricate detailing, making it a significant pilgrimage site for Buddhists and a marvel for tourists. Constructed entirely of terracotta bricks, each of the five main shrines is adorned with thousands of tiny Buddha statues, earning it the nickname "Temple of a Thousand Buddhas." The temple's unique blend of Hindu and Buddhist architectural styles reflects Nepal's diverse cultural influences. Visitors are mesmerized by the tranquil ambiance and spiritual aura of this sacred site, making it a must-visit destination for anyone exploring Lalitpur's cultural riches.

Begnas Lake is a gem nestled in the heart of the Kaski district in Nepal, adding to the natural beauty of the Pokhara metropolis. Situated southeast of Pokhara valley, it proudly holds the title of the third largest lake in Nepal, following in the footsteps of the renowned Phewa Lake among the eight lakes in the region.

What sets Begnas Lake apart is not just its size but the meticulous regulation of its freshwater through the western outlet stream, Khudi Khola. Spanning an area of 3.28 square kilometers and gracing an elevation of 650 meters, this freshwater haven offers a serene escape. With a maximum depth of 10 meters (33 feet) and an average depth of 6.6 meters, it invites exploration beneath its tranquil surface, revealing the wonders of its aquatic world.

Begnas Lake, with its picturesque surroundings and impressive dimensions, stands as a testament to the natural splendor that Nepal has to offer, making it a must-visit destination for those seeking tranquility and connection with nature.

Maulakalika Temple, located in Gaidakot, Nawalparasi, Nepal, is a revered Hindu shrine dedicated to Goddess Maulakalika, an incarnation of Durga. Maula Kalika Temple, perched on a hilltop in Gaindakot, Nawalparasi, is a deeply revered Hindu temple dedicated to the goddess Kalika, an incarnation of the fierce goddess Durga. The temple holds significant spiritual importance, drawing devotees from all over Nepal, especially during festivals like Navaratri, when the worship of the goddess is at its peak. The temple's location offers panoramic views of the Trishuli River and the lush plains of Chitwan, making it not only a spiritual destination but also a place of natural beauty. The hill on which the temple stands is believed to have been a site of meditation for sages in ancient times, adding to the site's mystical and historical aura.

Over the years, Maula Kalika has become more accessible, with a well-maintained staircase of approximately 1,600 steps leading up to the temple. This development has made it easier for pilgrims to visit, and the temple's infrastructure has been enhanced to accommodate the growing number of devotees. Besides its religious significance, the temple has also become a popular tourist attraction, contributing to the local economy. The Taleju Temple is one of Hanuman Dhoka Darbar Square's oldest structures. A "great temple" was built in 1563, under Mahendra Malla's rule, according to ancient diaries (tyasaphus) (r. 1560-74). Four notable structures, including the Jagannath, Kotilingeswar Mahadev, and Mahendreswara temples, are known to have been constructed at Darbar Square under the reign of Mahendra Malla. The Malla period building spree was financed by the kingdom's efforts to issue Tibetan currency for export and increase trade with other Himalayan kingdoms. The temple's current design resembles a cosmic mandala. The main structure has three levels of roofing and is supported by a base with twelve steps that resembles Mount Meru's lower slopes. There are sixteen satellite shrines built as two-story Newar towers all around the sanctuary. Notably, the main structure's roofs are covered in gilt copper sheets and supported by wooden struts with carvings of many gods. The temple is accessed by four portals—one on each side—each of which has a true door and two false doors. With carved wooden colonnettes, toranas over the main doorways, and pointed blocks (bhailahkva) flanking the lower door jambs, each is elaborately articulated.

Overall, the Taleju Bhawani Temple is a must-visit for those interested in Nepalese culture and history. The combination of its religious significance, stunning architecture, and connection to the Malla dynasty make it a true gem of Kathmandu Durbar Square.

The Taleju Temple is one of Hanuman Dhoka Darbar Square's oldest structures. A "great temple" was built in 1563, under Mahendra Malla's rule, according to ancient diaries (tyasaphus) (r. 1560-74). Four notable structures, including the Jagannath, Kotilingeswar Mahadev, and Mahendreswara temples, are known to have been constructed at Darbar Square under the reign of Mahendra Malla. The Malla period building spree was financed by the kingdom's efforts to issue Tibetan currency for export and increase trade with other Himalayan kingdoms. The temple's current design resembles a cosmic mandala. The main structure has three levels of roofing and is supported by a base with twelve steps that resembles Mount Meru's lower slopes. There are sixteen satellite shrines built as two-story Newar towers all around the sanctuary. Notably, the main structure's roofs are covered in gilt copper sheets and supported by wooden struts with carvings of many gods. The temple is accessed by four portals—one on each side—each of which has a true door and two false doors. With carved wooden colonnettes, toranas over the main doorways, and pointed blocks (bhailahkva) flanking the lower door jambs, each is elaborately articulated.
